item.title: Meet Franklin Howley-Dumit Serulle, whose online insect photo helped reveal a new hoverfly
item.description: An amateur naturalist's photograph on iNaturalist helped scientists identify a new hoverfly species. Researchers later found a specimen in Valle Nuevo National Park, confirming the discovery. This new species, Monoceromyia ndidiae, was formally described after laboratory analysis. The discovery highlights how amateur observations contribute to understanding biodiversity. This finding earned the Swiss Systematics Society’s New Species of the Year 2026 title.

item.title: 17 waste materials tested to make stronger, lower-carbon cement building products
item.description: A James Dyson Award project explores using waste for construction materials. Recycled aggregates like eggshells and glass replace conventional materials in cement. This approach reduces reliance on newly extracted natural resources. The project aims to create thinner, stronger cement boards and tiles. Further testing will assess durability and recycling potential for these innovative products.

item.title: Alaska saw 30,000 ship arrivals in 11 years; their hulls created a hidden invasive species risk
item.description: Researchers found that nearly 30,000 commercial vessel arrivals brought 430 sq km of submerged surface area to Alaska between 2012 and 2022. The study says this surface can carry marine organisms through biofouling. Passenger vessels accounted for more than half of the total area, while warming waters and increased Arctic shipping could raise the risk of non-indigenous species reaching Alaska.

item.title: Nepal’s flood bill could hit $5 billion. Where will the money come from?
item.description: Following the catastrophic floods, Nepal is staring down an enormous reconstruction cost running into billions. To restore infrastructure and homes effectively, both local resources and international assistance will play pivotal roles. The nation is actively pursuing funding opportunities with development banks and climate finance, emphasizing the importance of resilient rebuilding strategies for securing its long-term future.
item.dc:creator: Trisha Mahajan

item.title: In 2023, LA storms refilled shallow aquifers and reservoirs, but deep groundwater recovered only 25%
item.description: In 2023, record-setting storms brought a much-needed boost to Los Angeles's reservoirs and shallow groundwater levels. Yet, deeper aquifers, specifically those lying beneath fifty meters, showed only a slight recovery post-wet season, with just twenty-five percent of lost groundwater replenished. This highlights a crucial disparity; improvements in surface water do not mirror the health of underground reservoirs, a consequence of prolonged drought and aggressive water extraction.

item.title: Dutch scientists turn office urine into electricity, nutrients and potentially hydrogen
item.description: Men in a Dutch office toilet became a small power station using a dedicated urinal. This rig extracted phosphate and ammonia while generating electricity for electric cars. Bacteria break down organic matter in urine, transferring electrons to electrodes for current production. Separately collected urine is a promising feedstock for these bio-electrochemical treatment systems. Research shows urine can be a valuable source for fertilizer and hydrogen gas production.

item.title: In 2015, Canada sank a 113m warship off British Columbia; 170+ species lived on it by 2020
item.description: A former Canadian warship, HMCS Annapolis, now serves as an artificial reef. This vessel was deliberately sunk off British Columbia in 2015. Over five years, more than 170 marine species colonized the sunken ship. The artificial reef provides crucial habitat for various marine organisms. This project demonstrates the ecological value of prepared underwater structures.

item.title: California cleared 900,000 lbs of debris, but left old telephone poles for purple martins to nest
item.description: California crews removed more than 900,000 pounds of human debris while restoring about 40 acres at Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve. They also removed hazardous materials and old septic systems. Some telephone poles were left standing because purple martins use them for nesting. The birds were once thought to have disappeared from Santa Clara County.

item.title: Scientists image immune cells without dyes, detecting activation with 94% accuracy in 2 hours
item.description: A groundbreaking method has been unveiled by scientists that allows for the natural reading of immune cell data. This approach entails analyzing light emitted from molecules in immune cells, successfully distinguishing between activated and resting states with remarkable precision. By evaluating metabolism at the single-cell level without additional dyes, this technique promises to enhance our understanding of immune cell functionality and health.

item.title: In 2023, Australia paved two suburban roads with 135,000 recycled coffee cups and glass bottles, cutting the asphalt’s carbon footprint by 24%
item.description: Australia is embracing sustainability by turning discarded coffee cups into road materials. In Penrith, New South Wales, a groundbreaking project resurfaced local roads with a recycled asphalt mixture, incorporating approximately 135,000 coffee cups and countless glass bottles. This innovative use of recycled content has led to a significant twenty-four percent decrease in carbon emissions from the road surface, exemplifying a circular economy that creatively repurposes waste into valuable resources.

item.title: He spent thirty years transforming his 150-acre property into a wetland, now the former AP biology teacher is creating 'bio supermarkets' for wildlife
item.description: A former teacher is restoring Minnesota wetlands on his property. He has spent thirty years transforming his land back to its natural state. This restoration effort aims to combat significant wetland loss across the state. Wetlands provide vital ecological services and support biodiversity. His work is supported by the US Fish and Wildlife Service.
